title: A Mexican Christmas, a Colorado story: Mario Rivas and Nita Gonzales share holiday memories
summary: CPR Classical’s “Feliz Navidad” with host Mario Rivas brings together music from across Latin America and personal stories from Denver's Nita Gonzales, daughter of Chicano activist Corky Gonzales, for a celebration of family, tradition and the holidays.
content: Let’s do an experiment: Think of something associated with Christmas. Ready? Now raise your hand if you thought of Santa coming down the chimney. How about chestnuts roasting on an open fire, or sleigh bells in the snow? OK, now raise your hand if you thought of mariachi music. How about tamales, or Salsa Queen Celia Cruz?! No? Well, you might’ve raised your hand if you happen to be Latino… See, for all its similarities with the U.S., Christmas around Latin America can, and does, look and feel different. For one, several Latin American countries are in the Southern Hemisphere–where it’s summer in December–which means Frosty the Snowman would have to live either in the Andes or in your icebox. Latin American countries in the Northern Hemisphere are generally warmer and big cities get little-to-no snow. (You’d think Mexico City, at 7,300 hundred feet above sea level, would be a winter wonderland, but it’s bone-dry during the season!) Mix in indigenous, colonial, and African influences, add a dash of Catholicism, and it’s no surprise then that many of our holiday traditions are like our people–a little pious, a bit spicy, very colorful, and lots of fun! So, when I was asked to refresh “Feliz Navidad,” featuring holiday music and stories from across Latin America, I was more than happy to do it. I was, after all, born and raised in Mexico City. But, I’ll be honest, I moved to the U.S. over thirty years ago, so I’m now–according to my friends and family back home–a “gringo!” I immediately thought of my friend, social activist Nita Gonzales. Nita’s family traces her ancestry in Colorado to the Indigenous Peoples of the region. Her father was famed poet, activist, and Denver icon Rodolfo “Corky” Gonzales, founder of the Crusade for Justice in the 60s, a Chicano civil-rights organization that fought for social, political and economic justice in Colorado and beyond.). Every time I’m around Nita, I learn something new about the Latino experience in the U.S. and about the rich history of Colorado–one which she and her family have had a direct hand in forging. I was thrilled when she agreed to join me, and I hope you join us too. We share stories about food, family traditions, and memories of the holidays. You’ll also hear amazing, deeply personal remembrances of her father and mother, Corky and Geraldine Gonzales, and what it was like to celebrate the holidays in the middle of a political revolution. And, of course, the music will be front and center! We journey across Latin America to hear unique holiday music, like the aforementioned Celia Cruz doing “Jingle Bells,” some Tchaikovsky with a mariachi twist, and of course “Feliz Navidad,” by Jose Feliciano–whom Nita got to sing with! Now that’s what I call a Christmas miracle! title: Advocacy groups say Aurora court procedures violate a new state law
summary: In a letter sent to the Aurora city council and mayor in October, the ACLU of Colorado and Colorado Freedom Fund urged the city to fix the municipal code to protect the rights of defendants.
content: Advocacy groups in Aurora claim that the city’s municipal code and court procedures violate state law. Specifically, they are pointing to cases when it comes to the rights of defendants charged with crimes that carry penalties of jail time. In an October letter to the Aurora city council and mayor, the ACLU of Colorado and the Colorado Freedom Fund urged the city to change its municipal code. They want the city to follow the requirements of HB26-1134, also known as the Fairness & Transparency in Municipal Court law. It passed last April and seeks to bring fairness and transparency to the courts for defendants who can’t afford private counsel. The law clarified that municipal court defendants have a right to a public defender if the offense carries the possibility of jail time. The groups claim the city has not been offering public defenders to people in cases where the city decides not to impose jail time. In the letter, the groups said that by not offering counsel to those defendants, the city puts the constitutional rights of Aurora’s most vulnerable residents at risk. The groups argue the law was intended to prevent people from accepting uncounseled plea deals. They fear that without offering representation, those defendants will not receive legal advice on important aspects of their case. In the letter, they say the law requires people to be offered counsel when the offense has a potential of a jail sentence, even if the city has waived jail time. They added that both the written and verbal advisements the court gives defendants misstate Colorado law. “The Court must not advise defendants that they are ineligible for court-appointed counsel due to the City’s decision to not seek jail and must not advise those defendants that they are only able to obtain private representation,” the letter said. “Yet, as recently as August 7, 2026, Colorado Freedom Fund staff observed the Aurora Municipal Court advising defendants in this manner.” City of Aurora spokesperson Jennifer Soules confirmed the receipt of the letter from the ACLU and Colorado Freedom Fund. She said after receiving the letter, the city held a hearing to review how the law impacts municipal court policies and procedures. “In light of arguments and testimony delivered in that hearing, existing U.S. case law and applicable portions of the Colorado Revised Statutes, Presiding Judge Shawn Day ruled that the service requirements in the bill go beyond what is Constitutionally required and are therefore an unfunded mandate and optional under state law,” Soules said in an emailed statement. Soules declined to comment further, saying that the issue remains before the court and could be subject to appeal.

title: From the Black Sea to Colorado: A Christmas carol journey
content: “Carol of the Bells” is unmistakably one of the most beloved Christmas carols in the United States—but where did it come from? To find out, you’ll want to make sure your passport’s up to date, because we’re about to do a lot of international travel! With Carols Around the World, we take you all across the Northern Hemisphere, tracing the origins and stories behind Christmas classics. From the mysterious singing styles heard along the shores of the Black Sea to the wintry songs near the Arctic Circle, you might hear carols you’ve never encountered. Take a hike past the Alps to hear the astounding tenor of Luciano Pavarotti, find out which Iberian carol was sung by America’s legendary Dave Warland Singers, then come home to the sounds of Colorado with St. Johns Cathedral Choir of Denver. There’s so much to discover in the wide world of music. Come along for the ride and we’ll do more than just see the sights—we’ll hear the sounds as well—on Carols Around the World! title: Building wildfire-resilient homes can be made affordable, new research shows
summary: The study finds using cheaper materials can reduce costs
content: Wildfire is a constant and growing risk for homeowners in Colorado. While the cost of fireproofing can be a barrier, new research finds that building more fire-resilient houses can be made affordable. Colorado instituted wildfire-resilient building codes after the Marshall Fire in 2020, which destroyed more than 1,000 homes. Those practices can include replacing standard vinyl gutters with aluminum, installing ember-resistant vents, and replacing decks with ignition-resistant materials. Starting this summer , all new construction has had to meet minimum building standards to mitigate fire risk. The requirements are based on fire hazard risk, determined by factors like vegetation and topography. A new study from the University of Colorado Boulder found that homes that could be subjected to low-intensity fire hazards, like grassland fires, need protection from embers and direct flames. If the home is built in an area where it might be subjected to more intense wildfires, building designs should also account for radiant heat. The study assessed the state’s standards, along with more rigorous ones, and found the costs of meeting them only added between half a percent to about 11% of usual construction costs. “First of all, it’s very few components that need to be altered,” said Virginia Iglesias, an environmental data scientist and director of CU Boulder’s Earth Lab, who led the study. She found that key areas of a home that need the most protection are decks, vents, gutters and downspouts. Kevin J. Beaty/Denverite Lisa Hughes’ Louisville backyard is full of rocks and surrounded by a metal fence, part of her home’s hardening against wildfires. May 28, 2025. The study found that building wildfire-resilient homes can increase construction costs by $2,000 to $43,000. Driving the cost is often the selection of materials. Iglesias explained that the affordability of meeting these codes will depend heavily on cheaper materials being available regionally, and contractors being familiar with installing them. Asphalt shingles, for example, are much more affordable to install than metal. In Las Animas County, the total cost to build an average house ranges between $223,000 and $475,000, depending on the materials used. Building one to the new codes adds about 1 to 6% to the baseline construction cost. “It doesn’t cost a lot more to build to a wildfire resistance standard than not meeting those,” said Rebecca Samulski, the executive director of Fire Adapted Colorado, a nonprofit focused on wildfire resilience and post-fire recovery. “In fact, most of the practices in wildfire resistance standards are just kind of good construction to begin with,” she said. The study also evaluated the cost of meeting even higher standards than the state’s, including ones from the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety, a nonprofit that conducts building safety research. The costs associated with those standards were higher. Wildfire risk is increasing in Colorado. New research shows that the risk of losing a house to wildfire in the state could increase fivefold by 2050. While meeting state codes does not mean a house is fire-proof, it can significantly lessen the likelihood of a house catching on fire or burning down. In California, wildfire building codes reduced the risk of losing a house during a wildfire by about 40% on average. Courtesy: Vexcel Imaging U.S. Inc./vexceldata.com Homes in Beulah, Colo. burned in the Aspen Acres fire, seen via satellite imaging. Some insurers are also offering discounts for homeowners who take mitigation measures. However, state resources to help homeowners retrofit their homes are limited. A program created in 2023 intended to help homeowners pay to harden their homes, but ultimately only paid out $50,000 in grants before it was discontinued in 2026. Landowners also qualify for income tax credits for wildfire mitigation measures, but currently only through tax year 2027. Samulski said most existing incentive programs are “focused on the natural landscape and managing those landscapes we live in, not the landscapes that we’re building.” Some local governments are taking matters into their own hands. In Boulder , applicants are eligible for up to $2,000 to protect their homes. Douglas County provided grants this year for individual and community projects. “Most of the homes being built in Colorado are being built in areas that are vulnerable to igniting from wildfires, and we just haven’t quite caught up with that yet,” Samulski said. “We’re just starting.”

title: Your Guide to CPR Classical’s 2026 Sound of the Season
summary: CPR Classical's 2026 Sound of the Season is here!
content: CPR Classical’s 2026 Sound of the Season is here, with fresh ornaments for the tree. Mario Rivas hosts Feliz Navidad , an hour of music and stories from Denver, Mexico and Latin America. Mario is joined by Nita Gonzales, the daughter of famed Denver Chicano rights activist Rodolfo “Corky” Gonzales. They each share music, traditions and memories from growing up in Mexico and Denver. Pack your bags for Carols Around the World . Will Carman takes you on an international journey through the places and traditions behind favorite carols. Patty Painter-Wakefield brings a fresh perspective to December Solstice , with two hours of calming music for the Winter Solstice. The 18th Annual Carol Countdown , hosted by Kabin Thomas , begins airing Dec. 8. CPR Classical’s 12 Days of Carols starts on December 7. And each day, Scott O’Neil shares magical stories from Behind the Baton . CPR Classical midday host Monique Brooks Roberts produces and hosts The Spirit of Umoja: A Kwanzaa Celebration . Umoja means “unity” in Swahili and is the first of Kwanzaa’s seven principles, calling people to build and sustain unity in their families and communities. Monique explores how these principles that help a community thrive, can help each of us live a little more intentionally this holiday season. There’s more: We’ll illuminate the wonders of Hanukkah, celebrate Colorado holiday music and broadcast A Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols live from King’s College in Cambridge, England, on the morning of Christmas Eve. Metropolitan Opera broadcasts return Dec. 5. William Carman hosts CPR Classical’s annual Beethoven Bash to ring in 2027, and the Vienna Philharmonic’s New Year’s Day concert features Tugan Sokhiev, who will conduct the internationally broadcast concert for the first time.
